title: Setting up a rabbit colony run
subtitle: Housing rabbits as a loose group on grass rather than in individual hutches.
excerpt: A colony run is a large, fox-proof enclosure in which a group of does (and one or more bucks, kept separate) live on grass, in a structure more like a chicken run than a traditional hutch. Colony housing suits meat rabbits and allows rabbits to express more natural behaviours. It requires more space than hutch housing but less daily individual handling.
sourceNotes: RWAF, colony housing for rabbits (2022). British Rabbit Council, colony management guidance. Rare Breeds Survival Trust, smallholder rabbit keeping.

glossaryTerms.definition: A system in which rabbits are housed as a group in a large, predator-proof run on natural ground, rather than individually in hutches. Most suited to does of compatible temperaments, meat breeds, or non-breeding groups.

content.text: needs three things to work: enough space (at least 3 m² per rabbit), a predator-proof perimeter that extends underground, and the right group of animals. Rabbits in colonies establish a social hierarchy. Some aggression in the first few days is normal. Persistent bullying or serious fighting means the group composition needs to change.
3 m² per rabbit, with a minimum total run area of 12 m² for a group of up to four does.
A covered sleeping area or hutch section at one end, providing at least 1 m² per two rabbits.
Multiple feeding and water stations, so less dominant animals can reach food and water without being blocked.
Use weld mesh rather than chicken wire. Foxes pull open chicken wire; weld mesh at a minimum gauge of 1.2 mm resists biting and pulling.
Bury an L-shaped apron of mesh 30 cm deep around the perimeter and 30 cm outward horizontally to prevent digging. Foxes and badgers dig in rather than under; the L-shape deters them.
Cover the top of the run with mesh or solid roofing. Foxes, buzzards, and red kites can enter from above.

All-doe groups are easiest to manage. Add a buck only when you want to breed, and remove him immediately after mating. Intact bucks housed permanently with does will mate continuously, exhausting the does. Neutered male rabbits can be kept with does permanently and contribute to a stable group dynamic.
